ancient.name: Ain Ghazal 83-5
ancient.story_individual: AinGhazal 83-5 was discovered in the Ain Ghazal region of Jordan in one of the earliest and continuously occupied sites in the region. His remains were found among a cache of other mixed remains with limited additional information for contextual purposes. He lived approximately 8,600 years ago in one of the largest Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in the Near East.

ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

famous.name: Juan Vicente Pérez
famous.story_individual:
Juan Vicente Pérez Mora, born on May 27, 1909, in El Cobre, Táchira, Venezuela, was the world's oldest living man when he passed away on April 2, 2024 at the age of 114 years and 311 days. He was the last surviving man to have been born in the first decade of the 20th century, and the fourth oldest ever.

Pérez grew up in a family of farmers and started working in agriculture from a young age, harvesting sugar cane and coffee. He was essentially self-educated, learning to read independently from a book provided by his teacher who became ill and could no longer teach a few months later.

Pérez worked multiple jobs throughout his life in addition to agriculture, including that of a sheriff and on the construction crew for the highway between San José de Bolívar and Quenique. His tools were a pick and ax, and he was paid 2 bolivars per day.

Pérez married Ediofina del Rosario García in 1938, and the couple had eleven children together. Sadly, Ediofina passed away in 1998. As of his 113th birthday in 2022, Pérez had 41 grandchildren, 18 great-grandchildren, and 12 great-great-grandchildren.

Throughout his life, Pérez dedicated himself to farming, growing coffee, sugar cane, and vegetables. He attributes his longevity to a healthy lifestyle, which includes eating a diet rich in vegetables, drinking plenty of water, and getting sufficient sleep. Pérez also emphasizes the importance of maintaining a strong work ethic, a positive attitude, and, as a devout Catholic, a deep faith in God.

Pérez gained recognition as the world's oldest living man following the death of Saturnino de la Fuente García on January 18, 2022. His remarkable life and longevity have made him a celebrated figure in Venezuela, where flags flew at half-staff for three days following his death. He was an inspiration to many around the world.

His detailed Y-DNA haplogroup was determined by testing with FamilyTreeDNA by MAGENHA Project. The DNA test results were described in their video Don Vicente: Genealogía, Historia y Haplogrupos a los 115 Años.

Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2024) Claude 3 Opus [Large language model], and Wikipedia.

famous.name: Princess Maria Sviatopolk-Mirski
famous.story_individual:
Princess Maria Sviatopolk-Mirski (born in Meiningen, Germany) comes from the noble Sviatopolk-Mirski family, with deep ties to Belarus and Russia. She was born to Princess Nadezhda Ivanovna Sviatopolk-Mirskaya (1903-1983) and Prince Semeon Semeonovitch Sviatopolk-Mirsky (1910-1989).

The Sviatopolk-Mirski first appeared in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the late 15th century as "Mirsky", and has included Russian ministers and generals, and a Catholic priest who has been advanced by the Vatican as a candidate for beatification.

Princess Maria’s family's ancestral home was the historic Mir Castle in Belarus, which her great-grandfather purchased in 1895. Maria had two sisters, Anastasia and Irene, and a brother Sebastian who died young in Poland in 1942. The family lived in various European countries before settling in England in 1948, where they faced considerably reduced circumstances - her father worked as a painter and decorator while her mother worked in cafes and hospitals.

Princess Maria’s mtDNA was tested by FamilyTreeDNA at the 2010 “Who do you think you are?” live show in London. Apart from her familial connection to European nobility, her mtDNA is notable in that R0a (previously known as pre-HV) is a rare and old mtDNA haplogroup which occurs only in low frequencies in Europe.

Biographical information sourced in part from Debbie Cruwys Kennett’s blog Cruwys news. Profile photo sourced from Princess Maria’s X profile.

famous.name: Agnes of Waiblingen
famous.story_individual:
Agnes of Waiblingen, also known as Agnes of Germany, Agnes of Franconia and Agnes of Saarbrücken, was a significant figure in medieval German history as the daughter of Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV and a key link between several powerful dynasties. Through her strategic marriages, she played a crucial role in shaping European politics.

First married at age 14 to Frederick I, Duke of Swabia, she had several children including Frederick II of Swabia and Conrad III, who would later become King of Germany. After Frederick's death in 1105, she married Leopold III, Margrave of Austria, with whom she had at least 11 children, including Otto of Freising, the famous medieval chronicler, and several other children who formed important political alliances through marriage.

When her brother Emperor Henry V died childless in 1125, Agnes inherited the extensive Salian family estates. This inheritance, combined with her marriages and numerous offspring, helped establish both the Hohenstaufen and Babenberg dynasties as powerful forces in medieval Germany.

An interesting fact about Agnes is that her second marriage inspired a famous legend: her lost veil, found years later by Leopold while hunting, allegedly led to his founding of the Klosterneuburg Monastery, which became an important religious and cultural center.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was reported in Christiane Maria Bauer et al, Molecular genetic investigations on Austria's patron saint Leopold III, Forensic Science International: Genetics, Volume 7, Issue 2, 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2012.10.012

Biographical information sourced in part from Wikipedia and in part from Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large Language Model]. Pictured: 15th century painting of Agnes by Hans Part, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Liangdao Woman
famous.story_individual:
Liangdao Woman lived approximately 7,500 years ago on what is now Liang Island (also called Larne Island), located in the Taiwan Strait about 26 kilometers from mainland China and 167 kilometers from Taiwan. She was part of a coastal population living during the early Holocene period.

Her remains were discovered at the Liangdao site in the Matsu archipelago. Genetic analysis revealed that she carried mitochondrial DNA haplogroup R9, which is part of the larger Eurasian macro-haplogroup N.

The Liangdao Woman holds special significance as she represents the oldest genetic link between mainland Asia and what researchers call "Cordilleran ancestry" (referring to indigenous groups in the northern Philippines). Her DNA shows she carried a northern East Asian genetic component that was common in mainland populations, suggesting she lived during a crucial period of human migration in East Asia.

The location and time period suggest she was part of a maritime-adapted community, though we don't have direct evidence of her specific lifestyle. Her remains are particularly important for understanding early human migration patterns as they predate the spread of rice agriculture in the region by several thousand years, challenging traditional models about the connection between farming and human movement in ancient East Asia.

References

  • Larena, M., Sjödin, P., McKenna, J., Ebeo, C., Reyes, R., Casel, O., Huang, J., Hagada, K. P., Guilay, D., Reyes, J., Allian, F. P., Mori, V., Azarcon, L. S., Manera, A., Terando, C., Jamero, L., Sireg, G., Labos, M. S., Vilar, R. D., . . . Jakobsson, M. (2021). Multiple migrations to the Philippines during the last 50,000 years. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118(13), e2026132118. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2026132118

famous.name: Princess Diana
famous.story_individual:
Diana, Princess of Wales captivated the world not only as a member of the British Royal Family but also through her humanitarian work and charismatic personality. Born Diana Frances Spencer to Frances Roche and John Spencer, 8th Earl Spencer, she married Charles, Prince of Wales in 1981. During her time as a royal, she became known as the "People's Princess" for her charitable work and her ability to connect with the public. Her tragic death in Paris in 1997 led to an unprecedented outpouring of global grief.

Diana's legacy lives on through her two sons: Prince William, heir second in line to the British throne, and Prince Harry. Both princes have continued their mother's humanitarian work while forging their own paths in royal and public life.

In a fascinating genetic discovery made by BritainsDNA, Diana's maternal ancestry revealed an unexpected connection to India. Through DNA testing of Diana's matrilineal relatives, researchers identified that she carried a very rare mitochondrial DNA haplogroup classified as R30b. This genetic signature traced back to her great-great-great-great grandmother, Eliza Kewark, who lived in Surat, India, in the early 19th century. Kewark had formed a relationship with Theodore Forbes, a Scottish merchant with the East India Company, beginning a maternal line that would eventually lead to Diana.

The R30b haplogroup is remarkably rare, found in only 0.3% of the Indian population. Both Prince William and Prince Harry inherited this distinctive maternal genetic heritage, though as males, they cannot pass it on to their children. This genetic discovery not only highlights the diverse ancestry of the British Royal Family but also provides a tangible link to Britain's historical connections with India through the East India Company era.

References

  • A Royal Revelation - How BritainsDNA discovered Prince William's unknown genetic inheritance (Internet Archive)

Pictured: Princess of Wales (1983), Queensland State Archives, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2024) Claude 3 Opus [Large language model].

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.
